This afternoon through Saturday: A lingering localized shower 
and t-storm threat tonight and breezy and dry conditions this 
afternoon and Saturday mark the weather, along with the areas of
smoke. Low pressure centered near Vancouver Island migrates 
into southern BC and eventually Alberta by late Saturday night. 
A deformation axis stretches from the north-central WA/BC border
to north ID southward along the ID/MT border. This is where the
primary instability lays, with SPC analysis indicating CAPE 
values between 500-2000 J/kg, highest along the immediate ID/MT 
border, with mid-level lapse rates of 7-8 C/km and 0-6km shear 
values around 30kts. A dry slot has been coming in from the 
west-southwest, but there is still around 0.80 to 1.10 inch 
PWATs from near the Camas Prairie north into the Idaho 
Panhandle. With the low on the move providing a potential kicker
and the orographic lift, there is a risk for showers and 
t-storms over the NE WA and ID Panhandle mountain zones. The SPC
still shows a marginal risk for severe t-storms over that area,
with the risk for strong wind gusts and hail. The better risk 
appears to be in Montana, but this will be monitored. The 
potential continues this afternoon and tonight, though the risk 
shrinks to more northern Idaho and along the ID/MT border 
overnight.

There remains other fire weather concerns,, as the other 
feature of the next couple days is the wind and low relative 
humidity. The incoming low is helping to produce the combination
of wind gusting near 15-30 mph around the Methow Valley, 
Okanogan and Waterville Plateau. Regional RH values are in the 
20s to mid-30s, but the are expected to continue to drop through
this afternoon. Thus Red Flag Warnings are in place through 
this evening for these areas. Winds start to abate after about 9
PM, but we will monitor this to see if any of the winds linger 
beyond that time. The winds then start to pick up again through 
Saturday, with RH values dropping again toward the teens to 
lower 20s. The HREF joint probabilities of RH below 20 percent 
and winds at 15 mph is at about 30-50%, with localized spots 
near 60% the northern Waterville Plateau. We will continue 
highlight the elevated fire weather conditions for that.

Smoke is also causing troubles across some of the Inland 
Northwest. The southwest flow and multiple regional wildfires 
has be bringing smoke into much of eastern WA and north ID. Air 
quality has been in the unhealthy to hazardous level for much of
the Spokane Metro. State and regional air quality agencies have
issued air quality alerts, so check the Department of Ecology 
and other agencies for details. The smoke is forecast to 
continue to spread over southeast WA and over north-central WA 
near the northeast Waterville Plateau into Ferry county tonight 
into Saturday morning. The developing westerly flow per guidance
suggest the smoke will shift out of some areas and set-up over 
others heading through Saturday, so that it is focused over 
southeast WA to the central Panhandle (further away from the 
Spokane metro) and also focused from other fires near the 
northeast Waterville Plateau to northern Pend Oreille county. 

Sunday through Thursday: Low pressure will gradually lose its 
influence as a ridge of high pressure around the Four 
Corners/Central Rockies, but as we head into the middle to later
part of the week some more energy approaches from the Pacific 
and some monsoonal moisture begins to creep back in. Overall the
forecast is dry through at least Tuesday, then some shower and 
maybe some t-storm chances start creep back Wednesday onward 
mainly around the mountains. Highs are forecast to push into the
90s to low 100s by Tuesday onward, but the wildcard that may 
impact how warm we get may be any regional wildfire smoke. There
is also some spread among ensembles out the far, regardless of 
any smoke input with about 5 to 8 degree range between the 25 
and 75 percentiles. Either way the forecast is hot no matter the
precise number, with moderate to locally major HeatRisk by 
Tuesday. /Solveig
